summary: Summation No. 20 covers May 1947 (with much economic data for March-April), the month the new Constitution took effect on 3 May and the first Diet under it met on 20 May. After a month of interparty bargaining, Social Democrat Tetsu Katayama was named Prime Minister on 24 May and a three-party Cabinet was announced on 29 May. SCAP created a Reparations Section and a Reparations Technical Advisory Committee. The report details the Tokyo war crimes tribunal's defense case (China and Russian phases), Japanese judicial reform, and war crimes trials. Economic chapters cover record coke, steel and housing output, textile recovery, coal shortfalls, the abolition of the 700-yen wage limit, rationing, imports, finance and property control. Social chapters report health statistics, repatriation, teacher screening, religion and media. A historian will find dense monthly statistics and charts for tracking Occupation-era recovery.
highlights: Japan's new Constitution took effect on 3 May; MacArthur restored the national flag for display over the Diet, Supreme Court, Prime Minister's premises and the Emperor's residence.

The first session of the new Diet met 20 May: Tsuneo Matsudaira became President of the House of Councillors and Komakichi Matsuoka Speaker of the House of Representatives; the Ryokufu Kai formed with 90 members.

Tetsu Katayama was designated Prime Minister on 24 May by 420 to 6 in the lower house; on 29 May a three-party Cabinet of eight Social Democrats, seven Democrats and two People's Cooperatives was announced after Liberal talks failed.
General Orders No. 8 (8 May) set up the Reparations Section and No. 9 (21 May) the Reparations Technical Advisory Committee; ten nations had reparations delegations in Japan.

At the International Military Tribunal the defense finished the China Phase on 16 May and opened the Russian Phase, disputing responsibility for the Panay bombing and denying knowledge of Nanking atrocities.
April fish catch rose to five times March's on the herring run, while coal output in the first 20 days of May was 1,244,600 tons, 103,600 below the same April period.
The 700-yen wage and salary limit under the Emergency Financial Measures was abolished 1 May; Bank of Japan notes in circulation reached 129,685,000,000 yen on 31 May.
Two imperial ordinances created a Labor Standards Bureau in the Ministry of Welfare; about 400,000 workers attended Tokyo's quiet May Day; repatriates from 28 April to 31 May numbered about 69,700.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover for Summation No. 20 (May 1947), table of contents by part and section, and the list of 104 charts, maps and graphs.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of the month: SCAP reparations bodies, Constitution Day and the Katayama Cabinet, economic gains and shortages, and health, education and media news.

sections.title: Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: General Orders No. 8 (8 May) created the Reparations Section; No. 9 (21 May) set up the Reparations Technical Advisory Committee.

sections.title: Political Activities
sections.summary: Constitution Day on 3 May, new Diet officers, Katayama's selection on 24 May, the three-party Cabinet, public safety figures and war crimes trials.

sections.title: Economic Activities
sections.summary: Herring-run fish surge, coal and log trends, record coke and steel output, textile expansion, labor ordinances, rationing, finance and property control with the production index charts.

sections.title: Social Activities
sections.summary: Health officials' meetings, National Institute of Health dedication on 21 May, 3,181 hospitals, teacher dismissals, religious conventions, Constitution Week and Library attendance of 15,421.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Detailed reports on the Constitution, Diet and Cabinet crisis, public safety statistics, Japanese judicial reform, and the Tokyo tribunal's China and Russian phases.

sections.title: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Constitution Day, Diet organization, the May Cabinet crisis ending in Katayama's election and three-party Cabinet, party developments, neighborhood associations and the purge.

sections.title: Public Safety
sections.summary: Crime rose from 129,440 to 154,874 offenses in March, 134 killed in April rail accidents, prison deaths 1.6 per 1,000, and 2,107 fires in March.

sections.title: Legal and War Crimes
sections.summary: Provisional laws revised the courts, arrest rules and Civil Code; 90 suspects ordered arrested; 21 trials of 34 defendants; tribunal China and Russian phase testimony.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Twelve sections on production, transport, communications, labor, trade, rationing, finance and property control, with extensive statistical charts for March and April 1947.

sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Land reform progress and an April fish catch five times March's on a herring run gaining 357,017 metric tons; rope, salt and petroleum allocations.

sections.title: Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: April log output fell 88,688,000 board feet to 646,340,000; coal output slipped in May; lignite, oil drilling and mineral output covered.

sections.title: Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke at a 1946-47 high, postwar-high iron and steel, ferroalloys nearly doubled, housing peak of about 43,000 structures, chemicals, machine tools and machinery.

sections.title: Manufacturing
sections.summary: Food processing, paper, glass, electrical goods, leather and handicrafts; flour milling up with cereal imports, tin cans down for lack of tin plate.

sections.title: Textile Industries
sections.summary: Textile output kept rising from February through April in all branches except raw silk reeling; cotton, silk, rayon, wool and knit goods.

sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: More operable trucks and buses, slightly more train-kilometers but lower freight tonnage, rising shipping, plus electric power and gas data.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: Liquidation of International Telecommunications Company continued; telephone, telegram, radio, equipment manufacturing, personnel, finances and research laboratories.

sections.title: Labor
sections.summary: Imperial ordinances created the Labor Standards Bureau; May Day drew 400,000 in Tokyo; union conventions, disputes idle .19 percent of working time, employment.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Imports by commodity group (food, textiles, machinery, chemicals, metals, wood) and exports including 15,425,000 linear yards of cotton fabric to five countries.

sections.title: Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Rice collections of 4,222,100 tons since 30 September, imports 30 percent of the May ration, fertilizer deliveries, price increases and violations.

sections.title: Finance
sections.summary: Wage ceiling of 700 yen abolished 1 May; note circulation 129,685,000,000 yen; banks, deposit bureau, liquidation, Capital Levy collections of 16,650,000,000 yen.

sections.title: Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Looted ships (278 reported), allied and war-criminal property, German patents, zaibatsu holding company shares, rehabilitation expenditures and reparations delegations of ten nations.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health, welfare and repatriation, followed by education, religion, arts and media, ending with a map of Japan.

sections.title: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Communicable disease rates, veterinary affairs, hospitals, medical supplies, narcotics, relief to 2,763,041 persons, social security and repatriation from Soviet areas.

sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression
sections.summary: Teacher screening committees (120,000 teachers gone), religious conventions, cultural sites, radio, press, films with 475,637 attendance, theater, music, library, and map of Japan.
